opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For a small AI startup, I think the most important thing is people who are really hands-on and willing to go deep across the whole stack. In this field things move incredibly fast. A model architecture that was state-of-the-art six months ago might already be outdated. So I care less about whether someone knows one particular framework and more about whether they can learn quickly and get their hands dirty, from the hardware and systems layer all the way up to the application.

The second thing is a strong sense of ownership. At a big company you can be one piece of a very large machine, and that's fine. But at a startup there's no one else to catch things. If a customer's inference job is slow at 2 a.m., someone has to care enough to figure out why. I look for people who treat the product and the customer's problem as their own problem.

Third, I value pragmatism, a kind of engineering taste. In AI there's always a temptation to chase the fanciest research idea. What actually matters for a business is often making things reliable, efficient and cost-effective. Someone who can tell when a simple solution is good enough, and when it's worth investing in something harder, is extremely valuable.

Lastly, I care about humility and good communication. Our team is small, and many people come from different backgrounds, some from research, some from infrastructure, some from product. To work well together, you need to be open to being wrong, explain your reasoning clearly and respect what others bring. Technical skill gets you in the door, but those qualities are what make a small team work.

r001.rationale: The response says AI changes quickly and values learning over knowing one framework, but does not suggest prior experience is less applicable because the field is new to everyone.

r002.rationale: It values people who learn quickly and get hands-on across the stack rather than relying on familiarity with one framework, communicating willingness to engage with unfamiliar technologies.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about who I want to work with, a few things stand out.

The first is genuine curiosity. AI is moving so fast that whatever you knew six months ago is probably half obsolete. I care less about whether someone already knows a specific framework and more about whether they get excited when something doesn't work the way they expected. That instinct to dig in rather than shrug is hard to teach.

The second is what I'd call full-stack ownership. At a startup you don't have the luxury of saying "that's not my job." Back when I was building Caffe, I was writing CUDA kernels one day and answering GitHub issues from confused grad students the next. Someone who can move between the research side and the engineering side, and who actually cares whether the thing ships and runs in production, is worth a lot more than a narrow specialist.

Third, and this is maybe the most important, I look for people who are honest about what they don't know. In large companies you can sometimes hide behind process. In a small team, overconfidence is expensive. I'd rather have someone say "I'm not sure, let me check" than someone who sounds certain and is wrong.

And finally, I look for people who are kind. That sounds soft, but a startup is a long, stressful road, and you spend a lot of hours with these people. Technical brilliance doesn't compensate for making everyone around you miserable. The best teams I've been part of were made of people who were very demanding of the work and very generous with each other.

r001.rationale: The response says AI knowledge becomes obsolete quickly and values curiosity over knowing a specific framework, but it does not say prior experience is less applicable because AI is new to everyone.

r002.rationale: The response values digging into unexpected results, but does not clearly identify personally experimenting with unfamiliar technologies as a trait sought in colleagues.

astra-6.text:
I look for people who combine technical depth with a strong sense of ownership. In an AI startup, it’s not enough to say, “Here’s an interesting model.” You have to ask, “What problem does this solve for the customer, and what would it take to make it work reliably?”

I also value the ability to learn. The field moves so quickly that what you know today is only part of what you bring. Can you approach an unfamiliar problem, ask good questions, and change your mind when the evidence points somewhere else?

And then there’s collaboration. You want people who can disagree openly, explain their reasoning, and still work toward a shared goal. Especially on a small team, someone who makes the people around them more effective can have an enormous impact.

r001.rationale: The response says the field moves quickly and values learning, but it does not suggest that prior experience is less applicable because AI is new to everyone.

r002.rationale: It values approaching unfamiliar problems and asking questions, but does not identify personally experimenting with unfamiliar technologies as a trait sought.

sol-6.1.text:
I look for people who are curious, take ownership, and can turn an idea into something that works. In an AI startup, things change quickly, so being able to learn and adapt matters as much as what you already know.

I also value good judgment and collaboration. Can you identify the problem that actually matters to the customer? Can you explain your thinking, listen to feedback, and help the team make a better decision? You need technical depth, but you also need people who are willing to do the unglamorous work of building a useful product.
